lesson.title: Landing Exactly on k: Finding One Binomial Probability
lesson.summary: Finding the probability of exactly k successes without listing every outcome comes down to multiplying the chance of one specific arrangement by how many arrangements produce that count.
lesson.body:
Listing outcomes one by one works when there are only 3 trials, but the binomial distribution chapter already showed how fast that approach breaks down. What's needed is a way to compute P(X = k) for a specific value of k directly, using only n, p, and k, without writing out every possible sequence of successes and failures.

The idea splits into two pieces. First, because the trials are independent (one of the four BINS conditions), the probability of any one specific sequence with exactly k successes and n minus k failures, in some particular order, is just the product of the individual trial probabilities: p multiplied by itself k times, times (1 minus p) multiplied by itself n minus k times. Every sequence with that same number of successes has this same probability, regardless of which trials happened to be the successes, because multiplication does not care about order.

Second, since several different orderings can all produce the same count of successes, you need to know how many such orderings exist, then multiply the probability of one ordering by that count. That count, the number of ways to choose which k of the n trials are the successes, is what the next chapter formalizes as a combination.

Suppose a basketball player makes free throws with probability p = 0.7 on each attempt, independent from shot to shot, and takes n = 4 shots. What is the probability of making exactly 3? Label a make S and a miss F. The sequences with exactly 3 makes out of 4 shots are FSSS, SFSS, SSFS, and SSSF, so there are 4 such sequences. Each one has probability p cubed times (1 minus p) to the first power, since each contains 3 makes and 1 miss in some order: 0.7 x 0.7 x 0.7 x 0.3 = 0.343 x 0.3 = 0.1029. Multiplying by the 4 possible orderings gives P(X = 3) = 4 x 0.1029 = 0.4116. There is about a 41.16% chance the player makes exactly 3 of the 4 shots.

That pairing, the probability of one arrangement times the number of arrangements, is the entire engine behind every binomial probability calculation. For small n you can count the arrangements by listing them, as done here. For larger n you need a faster way to count them, which is exactly what the binomial formula supplies next.
